prompt: The shop's order API and its nightly report job are put in one Container Apps environment. Which of these do they share because of it? Choose all that apply.
hint: An environment is a boundary; think about what a boundary is drawn around.

choices.text: A virtual network
choices.why: Apps and jobs in one environment share its network, which is why they can call each other inside it.

choices.text: One revision history, so a new report image is a revision of the shop
choices.why: Revisions belong to one app; the report job has none of the shop's.

choices.text: A log destination
choices.why: Everything in the environment writes to the same place, a Log Analytics workspace by default.

choices.text: The shop's scale rule, applied to the report as well
choices.why: A scale rule is in one app's template and counts only that app's work.

prompt: The shop needs scale to zero now and may one day need a Dedicated profile for a heavier service. Which environment should it be given?
hint: One of the two kinds is labelled legacy.

choices.text: A Consumption-only environment, since only that kind scales to zero
choices.why: Both kinds have the Consumption profile and scale to zero; Consumption-only is the legacy kind and has no Dedicated profiles.

choices.text: A workload profiles environment
choices.why: It is the default, every one comes with the Consumption profile, and Dedicated profiles can be added to it later.

choices.text: Two environments, one per profile, joined by peering
choices.why: Different profiles can sit in one workload profiles environment; splitting them buys nothing here.

choices.text: A Dedicated profile from the start, to avoid moving later
choices.why: A Dedicated profile is billed per node whether or not the shop is busy, and Dedicated profiles cannot scale to zero.

prompt: The shop's app has external ingress with `targetPort: 8080`. On which port does a customer's phone reach it?
hint: `targetPort` describes the container, not the caller.

choices.text: 8080, the port named in the ingress
choices.why: 8080 is where ingress delivers requests inside, to the container. Callers never see it.

choices.text: 443, with port 80 redirected to it by default
choices.why: HTTP ingress answers on 443 under its own name and, unless told otherwise, redirects 80 to HTTPS.

choices.text: Whatever port Azure assigns to the environment that day
choices.why: The ingress ports are fixed: 80 and 443.

choices.text: 80 only, because TLS ends at the container
choices.why: TLS is terminated at the ingress, not in the shop, and 443 is the port that serves.

prompt: The finance export runs as a container app in an environment created with `--internal-only`. Its ingress is set to external. Who can reach it?
hint: Two settings: the environment's boundary and the app's place relative to it.

choices.text: Anybody on the internet, since external ingress publishes the app to the world
choices.why: External publishes the app at the environment's edge, and an internal environment has no public endpoint.

choices.text: Only other apps in the same environment
choices.why: That is internal ingress. External ingress puts the app on the environment's internal load balancer as well.

choices.text: Nobody, because the two settings contradict each other
choices.why: They do not contradict: it is Microsoft's documented way to keep an app off the internet but on the network.

choices.text: Clients in the connected virtual network, and apps in the environment
choices.why: An internal environment answers only on a load balancer inside the network, and external ingress publishes the app there.

prompt: A subnet given to a workload profiles environment has to be delegated to `Microsoft.App/___`.
hint: The plural of the resource this section's first half is about.

prompt: In the last 15 seconds, 1,500 requests reached a revision with an HTTP scale rule. What concurrency does Container Apps compute for it?
hint: The documentation divides a count over a window by the window's length.

prompt: A queue rule asks for one replica per 5 messages, with `maxReplicas` 20. One replica is running when 50 messages arrive. How many replicas does the next scaling step bring it to?
hint: The step is `min(maxReplicaCount, desiredReplicas, max(4, 2*currentReplicaCount))`.

prompt: A background worker has ingress switched off, no scale rule of its own and `minReplicas: 0`. What happens to it?
hint: With no rule, a default applies. Ask what that default counts.

choices.text: It runs one replica for ever, because zero needs a rule
choices.why: With no rule the default HTTP rule applies, and its minimum is 0.

choices.text: It scales to zero, and nothing will ever start it again
choices.why: The default rule counts HTTP requests, and with no ingress none can arrive.

choices.text: It is refused at deployment as an invalid app
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; it deploys, goes idle, and stays idle, which is why the documentation warns.

choices.text: It scales on processor load, the fallback for apps without ingress
choices.why: There is no such fallback. The default is HTTP, 0 to 10.

prompt: A report service is given a single custom rule on CPU load, with `minReplicas: 0`. Why will it never sit at zero replicas and still wake up?
hint: Think about what is measured when nothing is running.

choices.text: KEDA's CPU scaler does not reach zero alone
choices.why: With no replica running there is no processor load to read, so KEDA allows zero only alongside a scaler of another kind.

choices.text: CPU rules require multiple revision mode, which keeps one replica
choices.why: Revision mode has nothing to do with it; the scaler itself is the limit.

choices.text: A minimum of 0 is refused for every custom rule
choices.why: Custom rules on a queue scale to zero routinely; the documented limit is specific to CPU and memory.

choices.text: The cool-down period of 300 seconds never ends under load
choices.why: The cool-down applies when the last replica goes; the problem is starting again, not stopping.

prompt: Match each setting of the shop's scale block to what it decides.
hint: Two are limits, two are timings.

pairs.right: no usage charges while the revision is idle
the ceiling for one revision, not for the whole app
how often KEDA asks an event source, unused by HTTP rules
the wait after the last event before the last replica goes

right_distractors: how long a request may take before the ingress gives up

prompt: The shop's app is in single revision mode. Which of these changes creates a new revision? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask whether the change is inside `template` or inside `configuration`.

choices.text: `SHOP_VERSION` set to `1.1`, same image
choices.why: Environment variables are part of the container, in the template.

choices.text: A new value for the registry password secret
choices.why: Secrets are application-scope; running revisions keep the old value until restarted.

choices.text: `concurrentRequests` raised from 50 to 80
choices.why: Scale rules live in the template, so a new rule is a new revision.

choices.text: Ingress switched from external to internal
choices.why: Ingress is configuration and applies to every revision at once.

choices.text: A revision suffix of `v1-2`
choices.why: The suffix is part of the template, and naming one is itself a revision-scope change.

prompt: The shop's registry password is rotated and the secret updated. An hour later the running revision still uses the old password. Why?
hint: A secret belongs to the app; a revision read it once.

choices.text: Secrets take an hour to replicate across the environment
choices.why: There is no replication delay; the value is already in the app's configuration.

choices.text: The update made a new revision that has no traffic yet
choices.why: A secret change is application-scope and makes no revision at all.

choices.text: It read the secret when it started, and keeps that value
choices.why: It sees the new value only when it is restarted or replaced by a new revision.

choices.text: The password must be changed in the template instead
choices.why: Secrets are defined in configuration; the template only refers to them by name.

prompt: In single revision mode, a new revision of the shop never passes its readiness probe. What do customers see?
hint: Traffic moves only when something has happened.

choices.text: The old revision, which keeps all the traffic
choices.why: Traffic switches only once the new revision is ready, so a failed update leaves the old one serving.

choices.text: Errors until somebody rolls back by hand
choices.why: There is nothing to roll back: the traffic never left the old revision.

choices.text: Nine in ten on the old revision, one in ten on the new
choices.why: Single mode does not split traffic; that is multiple mode with weights.

choices.text: Nothing, because the old revision was deprovisioned first
choices.why: The old revision is deprovisioned only after the new one is ready.

prompt: A revision is an ___ snapshot of what an app runs: it is never changed, only replaced.
hint: The word for something that cannot be modified after it is made.

prompt: On the laptop, an order sent to the container for 1.0 did not appear in 1.1's list. With one revision and `maxReplicas: 10` in Azure, what would the same code do?
hint: Ask where `ORDERS` lives.

choices.text: Keep one list, because replicas of one revision share memory
choices.why: Replicas are separate processes, each with its own memory.

choices.text: Lose orders between replicas, since each one keeps its own list in memory
choices.why: An order sent to one replica is missing from the next one's answer; state has to live outside the container.

choices.text: Refuse to scale above one replica while it holds state
choices.why: Nothing in Container Apps inspects a process for state; it scales as the rule says.

choices.text: Keep one list as long as session affinity is switched on
choices.why: Affinity sends one client to one replica, but a second customer on another replica still sees another list.

prompt: Put the steps of the shop's canary in order.
hint: Nobody but the developers sees the new revision until the second step.
items: Deploy `shop--v1-1` beside `shop--v1-0` with the label `canary` and a weight of 0
Test it on the label's address
Set the weights to 90 and 10, and compare the two revisions
Move to 50 and 50, then to 0 and 100
Deactivate `shop--v1-0` once going back is no longer needed
trap: Deactivating the old revision as soon as it reaches 0 removes the one-command way back.

prompt: During the 90/10 split both revisions are active, and each has the shop's scale block with `maxReplicas: 10`. What is the most replicas the app can run at once?
hint: The limits are counted per revision.

prompt: The developers want to try `shop--v1-1` in the real environment before any customer reaches it. What does that take?
hint: One mechanism ignores the weights entirely.

choices.text: A weight of 1, the smallest a revision can be given
choices.why: Even 1 percent sends real customers there, which is what they wanted to avoid.

choices.text: A second environment holding a copy of the app
choices.why: That tests another environment, not this one, and the label makes it unnecessary.

choices.text: A label on it, and its own address, at a weight of 0
choices.why: A label's address reaches its revision whatever the weights say, including 0.

choices.text: Single revision mode, which tests a revision before switching
choices.why: Single mode tests readiness probes, not people, and then moves all the traffic.

prompt: The 90/10 split has been on for a minute. Twenty requests arrived and the canary received none. What does that show?
hint: Work out how often none out of twenty happens when everything is right.

choices.text: The split is broken, since two were expected
choices.why: Two is an expectation, not a promise; none happens about one time in eight.

choices.text: The canary is failing its probes and was taken out
choices.why: Nothing here suggests a failure; this is what a small sample does.

choices.text: The weights were silently rounded down to zero
choices.why: Nothing rounds a weight; the canary's share is exactly what the file says.

choices.text: Little: none of 20 happens 12% of the time
choices.why: 0.9 to the power 20 is 0.122, so twenty requests are too few to judge anything.

prompt: What does a blue/green release do that a canary does not?
hint: Compare who uses the new revision at each moment.

choices.text: It gives the new revision a share of real customers, rising in steps
choices.why: That is the canary: it trusts a few customers at a time.

choices.text: It moves every customer at once, after testing on the label
choices.why: The weight goes from 0 to 100 in one change; rolling back is the same change reversed.

choices.text: It needs single revision mode, where labels do not exist
choices.why: Blue/green relies on labels and weights, which are multiple-mode tools.

choices.text: It keeps both revisions at 50 percent until one is chosen
choices.why: That is an A/B test, not blue/green.

prompt: Which of these mistakes in `shop-app.bicep` does the compiler report? Choose all that apply.
hint: The compiler knows types and property names, not relations between values.

choices.text: `targetPort: '8080'`, a port written as text
choices.why: BCP036: an `int` was expected.

choices.text: `minReplicas: 5` with `maxReplicas: 0`
choices.why: Both are whole numbers; the compiler never compares one with the other.

choices.text: `concurrentRequests: 50`, a number in `metadata`
choices.why: BCP036: metadata values are typed as text.

choices.text: Weights of 90 and 20
choices.why: The compiler does not add weights up; only Azure would refuse 110.

choices.text: `activeRevisionsMode: 'Multi'`
choices.why: The property is typed as any text, so a misspelling compiles.

prompt: `bicep build` prints nothing for a file whose revision suffix is `v1.1`. What should you conclude?
hint: Separate what the compiler checks from what Azure checks.

choices.text: Nothing yet; only Azure checks the characters
choices.why: A dot is not allowed in a suffix, and nothing before Azure says so: check the rules yourself.

choices.text: The suffix is valid, since the build had no warnings
choices.why: A suffix is typed as text; the compiler checks nothing about its characters.

choices.text: The CLI would catch it before contacting Azure
choices.why: Without an account `az containerapp update` stopped at the login, before any check.

choices.text: Dots are turned into dashes when the revision is named
choices.why: Nothing rewrites a suffix; the template carries `v1.1` as written.

prompt: The nightly report should start at 23:30 in São Paulo, three hours behind. As a scheduled job, its cron expression is `30 ___ * * *`.
hint: Scheduled jobs read cron in UTC.

prompt: The nightly sales report runs for twenty minutes and exits. In Container Apps, what is it?
hint: One of the two kinds of resource stops on purpose.

choices.text: A container app with `minReplicas: 0`, woken by a request
choices.why: An app is restarted when it exits; the report would run again and again.

choices.text: A revision of the shop, with traffic weight 0
choices.why: A revision runs the shop's template; the report is a different program.

choices.text: A Container Apps job, with the Schedule trigger
choices.why: A job runs, finishes and stops, and a schedule starts one execution a night.

choices.text: A container app with a queue rule and `maxReplicas: 1`
choices.why: Scaling on a queue keeps an app serving; the report has nothing to serve.
